newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Senior politician quits in Hungary, denies scandal.
newsitem.headline: Senior politician quits in Hungary, denies scandal.

text.p: The head of the junior partner in Hungary's coalition government resigned unexpectedly on Monday but denied a financial scandal had anything to do with his decision.
Ivan Peto, president and parliamentary leader of the Alliance of Free Democrats (SzDSZ), told a news conference: "A change of leadership would benefit the party one year ahead of the elections."

Peto, a historian and founder member of the party, denied the decision was linked to a scandal involving millions of dollars in payments to Marta Tocsik, a former consultant to the Hungarian privatisation agency APV Rt.
"Tocsik has nothing to do with my resignation," Peto said.

Interior Minister Gabor Kuncze was named interim president of the party, whose popularity has plummeted in recent polls to less than 10 percent -- down sharply from May 1994 when it won a fifth of the seats in parliament.

Prime Minister Gyula Horn, whose Socialist Party has a majority without the Free Democrats, told reporters he was sorry about Peto's resignation but added: "I don't think this should affect or weaken coalition co-operation."
According to one party source, Peto's decision appeared to be linked to the unexplained payments of $5 million to Tocsik, who was hired to negotiate land deals in 1996.
Some of the money is alleged to have reached a businessman close to the Free Democrats and Peto has been criticised by opponents for not taking responsibility in the affair.
"He was obviously pretty unhappy that some of the SzDSZ people got their hands dirty in this whole thing," said political analyst Attila Ledenyi.
Other analysts said they did not expect the coalition government, which has already hit a trough in popularity, to be any further weakened by the resignation.
"I don't think that it has a very direct relationship with the stability of the coalition," said Istvan Stumpf, head of politics at the Hungarian Academy of Sciences.

"We are just one year before the election and the question is if these two parties, the Free Democrats and the Socialists, are able or are willing to create common strategy for the next election or they are running individually and independently.

"I think there are several people who would like to see much more independent policy and strategy from the Free Democrats' side and that could be one of the reasons why they would like to see Peto's resignation."
Peto, who will retain his seat in parliament, was one of a group of dissident intellectuals from the 1980s who founded the left-liberal party.

Western diplomats said that although the full significance of the change would not be known until a party leadership conference in May, it was clear that the Free Democrats were showing some independence from the Socialists.
"They are regrouping and getting ready for the election period that's starting," a diplomat said. "They are looking for ways to distinguish themselves from the Socialists."
